analysis.one_liner: Bars intimidation of election workers and presumes visible firearms near voters or poll workers are intimidation.
analysis.headline: A bill making it easier to sue people who intimidate election workers was introduced five weeks before the 2024 election, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Voting Rights Act to make it unlawful for anyone to intimidate, threaten, or coerce people who run federal elections — counting votes, certifying results, or working the polls — including because they used to hold those jobs. It would also create a rule in civil enforcement: if someone displays a visible firearm while near a voter or an election worker, a court would presume that is intimidation unless the person proves otherwise. Police on duty would be exempt. The House received it in late September 2024 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Election workers and officials — poll workers, canvass boards, vote counters, and election certification staff, many of them part-time or volunteer civic workers — plus voters at the polls. The bill gives them a federal civil remedy against intimidation and makes it far easier to prove by treating a visible firearm near election activity as presumed intimidation unless the person carrying it shows otherwise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Election workers, poll workers, and voters

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new Voting Rights Act provision making it unlawful for any person, whether acting under color of law or not, to intimidate, threaten, coerce, or attempt to intimidate anyone for administering a federal election, including vote counting, tabulation, canvassing, and certification, or because of their status as a former election participant.

Creates a rebuttable presumption in enforcement suits that displaying or carrying a visible firearm, imitation firearm, or antique firearm while interacting with or observing a voter, a vote-canvassing official, or an election worker is unlawful intimidation, unless the person proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.

Excludes law enforcement officers acting within their official duties from the firearm presumption, while still letting courts weigh their possession of a firearm in deciding whether they violated the intimidation ban.
Allows courts to grant relief including reasonable temporary limits on a defendant's carrying of firearms, giving judges a targeted tool short of broader weapons bans.

analysis.who_pays: People who display firearms near voters, poll workers, or election officials would face a legal presumption of intimidation they would have to disprove in court, and gun owners more broadly would see carrying near election activity carry civil legal risk. No public spending is involved; the bill adds no funding and no programs.

drawbacks.text: The firearm presumption shifts the burden of proof: once a person carries a visible gun near a voter or election worker, they must affirmatively show they were not intimidating anyone, which critics of such presumptions argue treats lawful, peaceful carry as a violation unless the carrier proves otherwise.

The presumption covers imitation firearms and even antique firearms, so someone with a prop, replica, or collector's piece near a polling place could face the same burden of disproof as someone with a working weapon.

The bill creates civil enforcement authority but provides no funding for election offices to increase worker security or training, so it addresses only the legal remedy side of the intimidation problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For election workers the benefit is concrete: a federal civil cause of action aimed directly at the threats and coercion that poll workers and canvass officials have faced, with an evidentiary shortcut for the most alarming scenario — a visible gun next to someone counting votes or voting. The cost falls on gun owners near election sites, who would bear a burden of proof they do not carry today, and the presumption's breadth (imitation and antique guns included) is the strongest good-faith objection. The bill contains no public spending, so the trade is between protecting election administration and narrowing how firearms can be lawfully carried around elections.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio and eight other House Democrats introduced the Freedom from Intimidation in Elections Act on September 25, 2024, about five weeks before the November 2024 election.
The same day, the House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee.
That was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who intimidate or pressure election workers face no new federal civil liability, and carrying a visible firearm near polls or vote counts carries no added presumption of intimidation; election workers remain covered only by the narrower existing Voting Rights Act provisions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Those who pressure election workers face no new liability

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on September 25, 2024.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 25, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee schedules
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor during the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine original sponsors and all eight cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled House Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Firearms owners and Second Amendment advocacy groups
industries.note: The bill would create a rebuttable presumption of unlawful intimidation whenever a person visibly carries a firearm — including replicas and antique guns — near voters or election workers, and would let courts temporarily restrict a defendant's carrying of firearms. Gun rights organizations characteristically oppose burden-of-proof presumptions targeting firearms display, though the bill regulates conduct at election sites, not manufacture or sales.

industries.industry: Election administration (state and local election offices and poll workers)
industries.note: The bill's new prohibition and evidentiary presumption would give election officials and poll workers a direct federal civil remedy against threats and coercion directed at administering elections. These are ordinary civic workers, not a profit-making industry, and their interest in the bill runs alongside voters' interest in secure elections.
